agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: EEOC (Title VII, 15+); state civil rights agency (lower thresholds)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 300 days EEOC (deferral state); 180 days (non-deferral)   |   State Range: 120 days (DE) — 3 years (NY, VT) — 6 years (MN private action)

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: Federal: 15+. State: varies — IL/MI/MN/WI/NY/NJ/VT: all employers

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: 42 USC §2000e (Title VII); 42 USC §1981 (race — no employer size min, 4yr SOL — CRITICAL for small employers); 42 USC §1983 (state actors)

elements.text: Plaintiff is member of protected race/color class
Adverse employment action (termination, demotion, failure to hire, failure to promote)
Plaintiff qualified for position or performing job satisfactorily
Causal link between race and adverse action (comparator evidence, direct evidence, temporal proximity)

proof_reference.text: McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting: prima facie → legitimate nondiscriminatory reason → pretext. Or direct evidence (stray remarks, documented bias).

fact_patterns.text: Termination after racial slur by supervisor; passed over for promotion despite higher qualifications than white peer; hired into lower-grade position than qualifications warrant; racially hostile work environment

barrier_reference.text: At-will doctrine; McDonnell Douglas pretext standard; arbitration agreements; mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts

intersections_reference.text: Sexual harassment (Title VII sex), disability (ADA), national origin (Title VII), wage gap (EPA)

remedies_reference.text: Back pay; front pay; compensatory damages (Title VII cap: $50K-$300K by employer size); punitive damages; reinstatement; injunctive relief. §1981: NO damage cap — critical for high-damage race claims.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: §1981 is the most important alternative to Title VII for race claims — no employer size minimum, 4-year SOL (Jones v. R.R. Donnelley), no damage caps, no EEOC prerequisite. Must prove intentional discrimination (no disparate impact theory). Critical for small employer cases.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: EEOC (Title VII, 15+); state civil rights agency

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 300 days   |   State Range: 120 days (DE) — 6 years (MN)

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: Federal: 15+. Most states: all employers

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Title VII; Bostock v. Clayton County (2020); Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins (1989); Equal Pay Act (all employers, 2yr SOL)

elements.text: Plaintiff is female (or male in reverse-sex case, or LGBTQ+ under Bostock)
Adverse employment action
Qualified/performing satisfactorily
Similarly situated comparators of other sex treated more favorably, or direct evidence

proof_reference.text: McDonnell Douglas (indirect) or direct evidence. Gender stereotyping as sex discrimination (Price Waterhouse). Bostock: LGBTQ+ = sex discrimination.

fact_patterns.text: Female employee paid less than male doing equal work; female terminated after pregnancy announcement; male supervisor favors male subordinates for promotion; transgender employee fired after transition announcement

barrier_reference.text: 2025: Trump EO directing EEOC non-enforcement of gender identity — state agencies critical for trans claims

intersections_reference.text: Pregnancy (PDA, PWFA), sexual harassment, race, national origin

remedies_reference.text: Same as Title VII race. EPA: back pay, liquidated damages (equal to back pay for willful), no EEOC prerequisite.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: For LGBTQ+ discrimination: Bostock is binding SCOTUS law but federal enforcement suspended by EO. State civil rights agencies in protective states (CA, NY, IL, NJ, MA, CO, WA, MN, etc.) are primary route. State courts remain fully available.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: EEOC (ADA Title I, 15+); state civil rights agency (many cover smaller employers)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 300 days   |   State Range: 120 days (DE) — 6 years (MN)

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: Federal: 15+. IL/MI/MN/WI/NY/NJ/VT: all employers

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: ADA Title I (42 USC §12112); ADAAA 2008 (expanded disability definition); Rehabilitation Act §501/504 (federal employees/contractors)

elements.text: Plaintiff has disability (physical/mental impairment substantially limiting major life activity)
Employer knew of disability
Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation OR accommodation was obvious
Employer failed to engage in interactive process OR denied accommodation
Accommodation would not have posed undue hardship

proof_reference.text: Interactive process failure analysis. Undue hardship defense: nature/cost of accommodation relative to employer resources. Regarded-as-disabled theory available without actual limitation.

fact_patterns.text: Denied modified schedule for chronic condition; denied remote work during recovery; refused leave as accommodation; forced return to work before medically cleared; terminated after exhausting FMLA leave

barrier_reference.text: Employer claiming undue hardship without actual cost analysis; failure to document accommodation request (always document in writing); EEOC often closes ADA cases quickly

intersections_reference.text: FMLA (leave as accommodation), mental health (MHPAEA if insurance), workers comp retaliation

remedies_reference.text: Title I: Back pay, front pay, compensatory, punitive (size-based cap), injunctive

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Mental health conditions (depression, anxiety, PTSD, bipolar) are disabilities under ADAAA. Employers must accommodate mental health conditions same as physical. Document every accommodation request in writing. Include statement: 'I am requesting a reasonable accommodation under the ADA.'

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: EEOC (all anti-discrimination statutes); NLRB (NLRA retaliation); DOL-WHD (FLSA retaliation); OSHA (25+ whistleblower statutes)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: EEOC: 300 days; FLSA: 2yr; NLRB: 6mo; OSHA: 30-180 days (statute-specific)   |   State Range: Varies by state retaliation law

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: EEOC: 15+; FLSA/NLRB: all employers

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Title VII §704; ADA §503; ADEA §623(d); FLSA §215(a)(3); NLRA §8(a)(4); Burlington Northern (SCOTUS 2006)

elements.text: Protected activity (complaint, charge, testimony, opposition to discrimination, participation in investigation)
Adverse action (materially adverse — not just minor, but anything that would deter reasonable employee)
Causal connection (temporal proximity; escalation after complaint; changed treatment)

proof_reference.text: Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. v. White (2006): materially adverse standard (broader than adverse employment action in substantive claim). Temporal proximity alone can establish causation.

fact_patterns.text: Terminated within weeks of filing EEOC charge; demoted after complaining to HR about harassment; hours cut after wage complaint to DOL; fired after telling coworkers about wage underpayment

barrier_reference.text: Employer documenting performance issues immediately after protected activity — preemptive documentation; arbitration clauses

intersections_reference.text: All discrimination claims; FLSA wage claims; NLRA concerted activity; whistleblower statutes

remedies_reference.text: All remedies available under underlying statute plus injunctive relief. Retaliation often stronger claim than underlying discrimination.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Retaliation is currently the #1 claim category at EEOC (approx 55% of all charges). Even if underlying discrimination claim is weak, retaliation claim may be strong if employer overreacted to complaint.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: DOL-WHD (FLSA, all employers in interstate commerce); state labor agency (many have higher minimums and stronger remedies)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 2 years (willful: 3 years)   |   State Range: NY: 6yr; MA: 3yr; IL: 3yr; CA: 3yr; most states: 2-3yr

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: FLSA: effectively all employers. No minimum.

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: FLSA 29 USC §206; state minimum wage laws; local ordinances (many cities $15-$20+/hr)

elements.text: Employment relationship (not independent contractor)
Hours worked at or below minimum wage
Employer failed to pay applicable minimum wage (federal $7.25/hr or higher state/local minimum)
Calculation of unpaid wages

proof_reference.text: Records-based: time records, pay stubs, bank records. Employer bears recordkeeping burden (FLSA). If no records, employee reasonable estimate accepted.

fact_patterns.text: Paid flat salary that works out below minimum wage; off-the-clock work required; tipped workers not reaching minimum wage; misclassified as independent contractor to avoid minimum wage

barrier_reference.text: Misclassification as contractor; arbitration agreements; fear of retaliation; immigration status concerns

intersections_reference.text: Overtime violations, tip theft, retaliation (FLSA §215)

remedies_reference.text: Back wages; liquidated damages (equal to back wages for willful violation — doubles recovery); attorney fees; injunctive relief. State: NY/MA triple damages.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Misclassification as independent contractor is primary wage theft vehicle. DOL 2024 rule narrowed contractor definition — more workers covered as employees. FLSA covers workers regardless of immigration status.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: DOL-WHD (FLSA); state labor agency

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 2 years (willful: 3 years)   |   State Range: NY: 6yr; CA: 3yr; MA: 3yr; IL: 3yr

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: All employers in interstate commerce

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: FLSA 29 USC §207; 29 CFR Part 541 (exemptions); collective action under 29 USC §216(b)

elements.text: Employment relationship (not exempt)
Hours worked exceed 40 in workweek
Employer paid straight time (not 1.5x) for overtime hours, or failed to pay overtime entirely
Employee is not exempt (executive, administrative, professional, outside sales, highly compensated)

proof_reference.text: Exemption analysis is key: employer bears burden of proving exemption applies. DOL salary test: exempt employees must receive guaranteed salary ≥ $684/week (federal, 2024 rule under review).

fact_patterns.text: Salaried employee misclassified as exempt; hourly employee told 'comp time' instead of overtime pay; off-the-clock prep/cleanup time not paid; multiple employer entities evading overtime count; rounding time records down

barrier_reference.text: Misclassification as exempt; off-the-clock work hard to document; arbitration agreements prevent collective action

intersections_reference.text: Minimum wage, tip credit, retaliation

remedies_reference.text: Back wages; liquidated damages; attorney fees. FLSA collective actions (opt-in) allow multiple employees to join single suit.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: DOL 2024 rule raising exempt salary threshold ($684/wk → $844/wk) stayed by court. Current threshold remains $684/wk pending litigation.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Employment   |   Primary Agency: NLRB (regional offices, 6-month SOL — precise)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 6 months from when employee knew or should have known   |   State Range: State labor laws supplement (some states stronger)

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: ALL employers — no size minimum

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: NLRA 29 USC §7 (rights); §8(a)(1)(3) (unfair labor practices); Weingarten rights (union representation in investigatory interview)

elements.text: Employee engaged in concerted activity (with or on behalf of coworkers) for mutual aid or protection
Activity was protected (wage discussion, collective complaint, organizing, union activity)
Employer took adverse action because of protected activity
No size minimum — applies to all workers

proof_reference.text: Concerted activity: need not involve union. Two or more employees acting together, OR one employee acting on behalf of others. Wage discussion between two coworkers = concerted activity.

fact_patterns.text: Fired after telling coworker their wage; terminated after group complaint to management about safety; discharged after organizing coworkers around scheduling concerns; fired for social media post about working conditions with coworkers

barrier_reference.text: Agricultural workers, domestic workers, independent contractors excluded from NLRA; supervisors excluded

intersections_reference.text: Wage retaliation (FLSA), race/sex discrimination (Title VII), immigration status (irrelevant — NLRA covers all workers)

remedies_reference.text: Reinstatement; back pay; cease and desist order. Limited remedies by design — punitive damages not available. Value is in protecting organizing rights.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: NLRB enforcement capacity reduced 2025 (fired board members, reduced staff). File charges to preserve rights even if enforcement uncertain. NLRB charge filing date is critical for SOL. NLRA is the MOST POWERFUL tool for workers at small employers who fall below all civil rights thresholds.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Housing   |   Primary Agency: HUD (FHA, 1yr); state civil rights agency; federal court (2yr)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: HUD: 1 year; federal court: 2 years   |   State Range: Most states: 1-2 years

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — applies to housing providers; exemptions: owner-occupied ≤4 units (Mrs. Murphy), private clubs, religious organizations

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Fair Housing Act 42 USC §3601-3631; Texas Dept. of Housing v. Inclusive Communities Project (2015, disparate impact)

elements.text: Plaintiff is member of protected class (race, color, national origin)
Sought housing (rental, purchase, or financing)
Denied, discouraged, offered inferior terms, or subjected to different treatment
Defendant's conduct was because of protected class

proof_reference.text: Disparate treatment (direct/indirect evidence) or disparate impact (neutral policy with discriminatory effect, Inclusive Communities). Steering, blockbusting, and redlining are per se violations.

fact_patterns.text: Apartment shown but then told 'unavailable' after meeting applicant; different terms offered to white vs. minority applicants; told 'neighborhood isn't right for you'; Hispanic applicant required to provide documentation white applicant was not

barrier_reference.text: Proving intent without direct evidence; landlord claiming legitimate non-discriminatory reason (higher income applicant, better credit); pretextual rejection

intersections_reference.text: Source of income (Section 8 — not federal, state/local only), disability accommodation, familial status, VAWA

remedies_reference.text: Actual damages; compensatory damages; punitive damages; injunctive relief; attorney fees. HUD: up to $16,000 civil penalty per violation.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: HUD remains functional for FHA enforcement. Source of income discrimination (denying Section 8/voucher holders) is not covered by federal FHA — covered in ~20 states and many cities. Flag every housing case for local SOI coverage.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Housing   |   Primary Agency: HUD (FHA); state civil rights agency; DOJ (public housing authorities — ADA Title II)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 1 year (HUD)   |   State Range: 1-2 years typically

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: FHA §3604(f)(3)(B); Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (HUD/DOJ 2004)

elements.text: Person has disability (broadly defined under FHA amendments)
Requested accommodation (policy change) or modification (structural change)
Accommodation/modification is reasonable (not fundamental alteration or undue burden)
Housing provider refused or failed to engage in interactive process

proof_reference.text: FHA disability accommodation: two-part test — (1) disability-related need, (2) accommodation is reasonable. Provider can request documentation but cannot demand medical records for obvious disability.

fact_patterns.text: Denied emotional support animal in no-pet building; denied first-floor apartment for mobility impairment; refused permission to install grab bars; evicted after disability-related behavior incident without accommodation consideration

barrier_reference.text: ESA documentation scams — document from treating provider; housing provider demanding excessive documentation

intersections_reference.text: Section 504 (federally funded housing), ADA Title II (public housing authorities)

remedies_reference.text: Same as FHA. Civil penalties escalate for repeat violations.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Emotional support animals (ESAs) are a major litigation area. FHA does NOT allow breed/weight restrictions for ESAs even if prohibited in lease. Provider may verify disability nexus only for non-obvious disabilities. HUD updated ESA guidance 2020 — providers may request documentation from treating provider.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Housing   |   Primary Agency: State civil rights agency (where SOI covered); local human rights commission; HUD (limited federal coverage via nondiscrimination conditions on HUD-funded landlords)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: N/A (not federal FHA protected class)   |   State Range: Varies — check jurisdiction

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: State laws: CA, OR, WA, CO, MN, IL (Chicago), NY, NJ, CT, MA, RI, VT, ME, MD, DC, DE, ND, NE (Lincoln), TX (Austin, Dallas), FL (no state law but some cities)

elements.text: Plaintiff holds housing voucher (Section 8/HCV, other rental assistance)
Landlord refused to rent, accept voucher, or offered inferior terms because of voucher status
Jurisdiction covers source of income as protected class

proof_reference.text: Direct evidence (landlord stated no Section 8); circumstantial (available to all applicants except voucher holders).

fact_patterns.text: 'No Section 8' in rental ad; told voucher is accepted then rejected after learning it is voucher; steered to lower-quality units

barrier_reference.text: No federal remedy; must identify local coverage; landlords often claim other reasons

intersections_reference.text: Race discrimination (voucher holders disproportionately minority — can argue Title VIII pretext)

remedies_reference.text: Varies by jurisdiction: actual damages, civil penalties, injunctive relief

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Source of income protection growing: multiple cities added SOI protection 2024-25. Always check current local ordinances. Where SOI not covered, consider whether race/national origin discrimination underlies voucher rejection.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Housing   |   Primary Agency: HUD (VAWA protections); state DV coalitions; local housing authority

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: HUD: 1 year. Emergency transfer: immediate.   |   State Range: Varies

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: VAWA Reauthorization Act 2022; 24 CFR Part 5 Subpart L (HUD VAWA regulations); HUD VAWA emergency transfer plan requirements

elements.text: Person is victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking
Housing is federally funded (public housing, Section 8/HCV, HOME, HOPWA, VAWA-covered programs)
Landlord attempted to evict or penalize victim for incidents related to DV/SA/stalking, OR denied emergency transfer

proof_reference.text: VAWA self-certification: victim can self-certify victimhood on HUD form. Provider cannot require police report or court order. Emergency transfer request: provider must document transfer plan within 14 days.

fact_patterns.text: Eviction notice after DV incident in unit; lease termination after 911 calls; denied transfer to safe unit; bifurcated lease to evict abuser

barrier_reference.text: Private landlords not covered (only federally funded programs); victim may not know federal housing receives VAWA protection

intersections_reference.text: FHA disability (PTSD from DV), sex discrimination (DV disproportionately affects women)

remedies_reference.text: Injunctive relief (stop eviction); emergency transfer; VAWA certification as defense to eviction

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: VAWA 2022 expanded protections. HUD issued updated VAWA regulations. Emergency transfer right is strongest immediate protection — do not wait for investigation.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Housing   |   Primary Agency: State court (primary remedy — emergency TRO/injunction); state AG consumer protection; local tenant protection agencies

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: N/A   |   State Range: Emergency injunction: same day — act immediately

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: State landlord-tenant laws; state consumer protection acts; URLTA (adopted in ~20 states)

elements.text: Landlord-tenant relationship
Landlord engaged in self-help eviction: changed locks, removed belongings, shut off utilities, or constructively evicted without court order
Tenant did not voluntarily vacate

proof_reference.text: Self-help eviction is illegal in almost all U.S. jurisdictions. Landlord must use judicial eviction process. Emergency injunction is primary remedy.

fact_patterns.text: Locks changed without eviction proceeding; utilities shut off; belongings placed in street; intimidation/harassment to force out

barrier_reference.text: Tenant may not know legal eviction requires court process; undocumented tenants may fear reporting

intersections_reference.text: FHA (if discrimination nexus), VAWA (DV context), municipal tenant protection ordinances

remedies_reference.text: Emergency TRO (immediate restoration of possession); actual damages; punitive damages in many states; attorney fees

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Post-pandemic eviction moratorium landscape: most federal/state moratoria expired but some local protections remain. Check local just-cause eviction requirements (CA, NJ, NY, WA, OR, NM, and many cities require just cause).

claims.canonical_name: ADA Title II — Discrimination by State/Local Government
claims.identity_basis: Manually reconciled source identifier and full claim title to the retrieved claim_catalog row; existing ID retained.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Disability   |   Primary Agency: DOJ (enforcement — capacity reduced 2025); relevant federal agency (ED-OCR for schools, HHS-OCR for public health programs); federal court private action

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 2 years (federal court); 180 days (agency complaint)   |   State Range: State Rehabilitation Act equivalents

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — applies to all public entities regardless of size

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: ADA Title II 42 USC §12131; Olmstead v. L.C. (1999, community integration mandate); Tennessee v. Lane (2004, courts); US v. Georgia (2006, prisons)

elements.text: Plaintiff has disability
Defendant is public entity (state, local government, court, DMV, jail, transit system, school district)
Plaintiff was excluded from program, service, or activity, OR denied equal access
Exclusion was by reason of disability

proof_reference.text: Title II does not require showing comparator. Failure to provide effective communication (sign language, captioning, large print) is per se violation. Failure to make reasonable modification to policies is violation.

fact_patterns.text: Courthouse inaccessible for wheelchair user; DMV unable to provide sign language interpreter; jail refusing medication for psychiatric condition; transit system inaccessible; court documents not available in accessible format

barrier_reference.text: Sovereign immunity (states): Title II creates private right of action and abrogates sovereign immunity for most violations. Title II suits against states possible.

intersections_reference.text: Section 504, Olmstead integration mandate, mental health system rights

remedies_reference.text: Injunctive relief (primary); compensatory damages (requires showing intentional discrimination for damages against state); attorney fees

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: DOJ Title II enforcement reduced. State-level disability rights organizations and protection and advocacy (P&A) systems are primary enforcement resources. P&A organizations have federally mandated access to facilities and records.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Disability   |   Primary Agency: DOJ (enforcement); federal court (private action — 2 years)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 2 years   |   State Range: Varies

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — ALL public accommodations

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: ADA Title III 42 USC §12182; ADA Accessibility Guidelines (ADAAG); website accessibility (DOJ rule: WCAG 2.1 AA, effective 2026 for larger entities)

elements.text: Defendant is place of public accommodation (hotel, restaurant, retail, hospital, school, gym, theater, doctor's office — essentially all private businesses open to public)
Plaintiff has disability
Plaintiff denied full and equal enjoyment due to failure to remove barrier or modify policy
Removal of barrier was readily achievable

proof_reference.text: No employer size minimum. No disparate impact in ADA Title III — must show denial of access. Readily achievable standard: easily accomplished without much difficulty or expense.

fact_patterns.text: Restaurant with no accessible entrance; pharmacy with inaccessible checkout counter; doctor's office refusing to provide sign language interpreter; hotel room not actually accessible as advertised; website inaccessible to screen reader

barrier_reference.text: Religious organizations and private clubs exempt from Title III

intersections_reference.text: Section 1557 (healthcare), FHA (if housing component), state disability access laws (CA Unruh Act — stronger remedies)

remedies_reference.text: Injunctive relief (primary in federal court — no individual damages for Title III!); attorney fees. CA Unruh Act: $4,000 per violation + actual damages — much stronger.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Website and app accessibility now major litigation area. DOJ finalized rule (Apr 2024) requiring WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance for state/local government websites (Title II) — effective 2026-2027. Private businesses (Title III) no mandatory standard yet but DOJ guidance.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Disability   |   Primary Agency: DOJ (Olmstead enforcement — capacity reduced 2025); state P&A system; state developmental disabilities agency; federal court §1983/Title II

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: No SOL for ongoing violation   |   State Range: N/A for ongoing institutionalization

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — state programs

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: ADA Title II; Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999); 28 CFR §35.130(d) (integration regulation)

elements.text: Person with mental or physical disability currently institutionalized or at serious risk of institutionalization
State provides services to people with disabilities in community settings
Community placement is appropriate for person's condition
Person does not oppose community placement
Community placement can be reasonably accommodated given state's resources

proof_reference.text: Olmstead v. L.C. (1999): ADA Title II integration mandate requires states to provide services in most integrated setting appropriate. States must have plan for moving people out of institutions.

fact_patterns.text: Person with developmental disability waitlisted for community placement for years while institutionalized; person with mental health condition discharged from hospital to homeless/jail rather than community support; state cutting HCBS waiver

barrier_reference.text: Budget constraints defense; complexity of state Medicaid waiver system

intersections_reference.text: Mental health system pipeline, Medicaid HCBS waivers, disability rights

remedies_reference.text: Injunctive relief requiring state to provide community placement; systemic reform; attorney fees

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Olmstead enforcement by DOJ significantly reduced. State P&A organizations and disability rights legal organizations (e.g., National Disability Rights Network members) are primary advocates. Medicaid HCBS waiver cuts are a growing Olmstead issue.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Education   |   Primary Agency: State educational agency (due process hearing); ED-OCR (procedural violations); federal court (IDEA appeal — 2yr SOL from knew/should have known)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: Due process: 2yr state SOL typically; ED-OCR: 180 days   |   State Range: 2 years most states; some shorter

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: IDEA 20 USC §1400; Endrew F. v. Douglas County (2017); Florence County School District v. Carter (1993, private placement reimbursement); Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools (2017, exhaustion)

elements.text: Child has disability that adversely affects educational performance
Child has right to free appropriate public education (FAPE) in least restrictive environment (LRE)
School failed to provide FAPE (inadequate IEP, failure to implement IEP, denial of services, inappropriate placement)
Parent/guardian has procedural rights (IEP meetings, prior written notice, independent evaluation)

proof_reference.text: Endrew F. v. Douglas County (2017): IEP must be 'reasonably calculated to enable child to make progress appropriate in light of circumstances.' Two-part test.

fact_patterns.text: Child not evaluated for disability despite parent request; IEP not implemented by school; child placed in segregated setting without FAPE analysis; parent excluded from IEP meeting; extended school year denied

barrier_reference.text: Administrative exhaustion required before court. Due process hearing is first step — legal aid essential for hearings.

intersections_reference.text: Section 504 (disability), Title VI (race disproportionality in special ed), Title IX (disability intersecting sex)

remedies_reference.text: Compensatory services; private school placement reimbursement; attorney fees (when parent substantially prevails). No punitive damages.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: IDEA funding disputes ongoing. Disproportionate representation of minority students in special education (both over- and under-identification) is a Title VI/IDEA intersection issue.

claims.canonical_name: Title IX — Sexual Harassment/Assault in Educational Setting
claims.identity_basis: Manually reconciled source identifier and full claim title to the retrieved claim_catalog row; existing ID retained.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Education   |   Primary Agency: ED-OCR (180 days); federal court private action (state SOL, typically 2-3 years)

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: ED-OCR: 180 days; federal court: state SOL   |   State Range: Typically 2-3 years (state personal injury SOL)

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — any recipient of federal education funding

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Title IX 20 USC §1681; Gebser v. Lago Vista (1998); Davis v. Monroe County (1999); Cummings v. Premier Rehab (2022, emotional distress damages limited under Spending Clause statutes)

elements.text: Institution receives federal funding
Plaintiff experienced sexual harassment or assault
Institution had actual knowledge of harassment
Institution was deliberately indifferent to known harassment
Harassment denied plaintiff equal access to educational program

proof_reference.text: Gebser/Davis standard: actual knowledge + deliberate indifference. Newer: hostile environment test (severe, pervasive, objectively offensive). School may be liable for employee-on-student harassment differently than peer-on-peer.

fact_patterns.text: Student assaulted by another student; school failed to investigate; survivor punished for reporting; survivor forced to share class with assailant; school failed to provide supportive measures

barrier_reference.text: 2025: Title IX regulations under revision by Trump administration (reverting to pre-Biden guidance). Deliberate indifference standard is high bar. OCR enforcement reduced.

intersections_reference.text: Title VII (employees), state tort (negligence, assault), state DFCS/child protective services

remedies_reference.text: Compensatory damages; injunctive relief; attorney fees. Note: Cummings (2022) may limit emotional distress damages in Spending Clause cases — circuit split.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Trump admin rescinded Biden 2022 Title IX regs. 2020 DeVos regs back in effect (more protective of accused). OCR enforcement reduced — state education agencies and private litigation are primary routes.

Communication was in connection with collection of debt

fact_patterns.text: Collector calling employer; threatening arrest for civil debt; collecting debt past SOL without disclosure; threatening to sue when not actually planning to; contacting person who has attorney

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: EMTALA 42 USC §1395dd; Roberts v. Galen (1999, no discriminatory motive required)

Patient presented to emergency department seeking treatment
Hospital failed to provide appropriate medical screening examination
Hospital transferred/discharged patient in unstable condition, OR refused to accept appropriate transfer from another hospital

proof_reference.text: EMTALA is not an anti-discrimination statute — it requires equal screening and stabilization for all patients regardless of payment ability. Proof of disparate screening compared to other patients is key.

fact_patterns.text: ER patient denied treatment because no insurance and told to leave; pregnant patient turned away before evaluation; psychiatric patient discharged before stabilized; hospital refusing to accept transfer of uninsured patient

barrier_reference.text: EMTALA private right of action limited; hospital physician immunity in some states; medical expert required for malpractice component

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: EMTALA and emergency abortion: post-Dobbs conflict between EMTALA (requires stabilizing care including pregnancy complications) and state abortion bans. Still unresolved in several circuits.

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: ERISA: typically 3 years; state insurance: varies   |   State Range: State parity laws often stronger: CA, NY, IL, MA, WA, OR

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A — insurer/plan

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: MHPAEA 29 USC §1185a; ACA (expanded parity to individual and small group); 2024 Final Rule (DOL/CMS/Treasury) strengthening NQTL requirements; state parity laws

elements.text: Insurance plan subject to MHPAEA (employer group health plans, Medicaid MCOs, most marketplace plans)
Plan provides mental health or SUD benefits
Plan applied more restrictive limitations on MH/SUD than on medical/surgical benefits
Limitation applied in ways that are not comparable and are not applied no more stringently

proof_reference.text: Comparative analysis: what limitations apply to MH/SUD vs. analogous medical/surgical benefits? Prior authorization for SUD treatment when not required for comparable medical treatment = likely parity violation. Nonquantitative treatment limitations (NQTLs) require rigorous comparative analysis.

fact_patterns.text: Residential SUD treatment denied while medical hospitalization covered; psychiatrist visit limit when no specialist visit limit for physical conditions; prior auth required for every SUD session; out-of-network SUD reimbursement lower than medical

barrier_reference.text: ERISA preempts state law claims for self-funded employer plans; complexity of NQTL analysis; need for actuary or parity expert

intersections_reference.text: Medicaid (CMS enforcement), disability discrimination (denial of SUD treatment as disability discrimination)

remedies_reference.text: ERISA: equitable relief (payment of denied benefits), attorney fees. State: varies. 2024 rule requires plans to perform and document NQTL analysis — document requests now available.

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: 2024 DOL/CMS/Treasury Final Rule on parity is in effect. Plans must perform documented comparative analysis of NQTLs. Request plan's NQTL analysis as first step in parity violation investigation.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Benefits   |   Primary Agency: State Medicaid agency (fair hearing — exhaust first); CMS (systemic); federal court §1983 after exhaustion

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: Fair hearing request: typically 90 days from notice (some states 30 days — check immediately)   |   State Range: 90 days most states; federal court after exhaustion

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Social Security Act §1902 (Medicaid); 42 USC §1396a; Goldberg v. Kelly (1970, due process); Edelman v. Jordan (state must repay wrongfully withheld benefits)

elements.text: Applicant/recipient is eligible for Medicaid under applicable state plan and federal law
State denied, terminated, or reduced benefits without adequate basis
Adequate notice was not provided (10 days advance notice required for planned action)
Fair hearing right was not afforded

proof_reference.text: Due process: Mathews v. Eldridge balancing test. State must provide: adequate written notice stating specific reason; opportunity to request fair hearing; continuation of benefits pending hearing if requested timely.

fact_patterns.text: Medicaid terminated without notice; managed care organization denied service authorization; HCBS waiver terminated; benefits reduced without individualized assessment; agency applied wrong income calculation

barrier_reference.text: Fair hearing deadlines are absolute — missing them usually bars further appeal. Claimants often don't know rights. Request continuation of benefits when requesting hearing.

intersections_reference.text: Olmstead (community integration), MHPAEA (parity in managed care), disability rights

remedies_reference.text: Reinstatement of benefits; back payment of wrongfully denied benefits; attorney fees in some §1983 circuits

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Medicaid redeterminations following COVID continuous enrollment ended 2023-24. Millions disenrolled. Many disenrollments were procedurally improper — strong fair hearing cases for improper termination.

elements.text: Household is eligible based on income/resource limits
State denied or terminated SNAP without basis
Notice was inadequate or hearing right denied
Expedited (emergency) processing was not provided when required (within 7 days for eligible households)

proof_reference.text: Eligibility analysis: gross income test, net income test, resource test, categorical eligibility. Expedited households: gross monthly income under $150 AND liquid resources under $100, OR combined income and resources less than monthly rent/mortgage AND utilities.

fact_patterns.text: SNAP denied based on categorical eligibility interpretation error; benefits terminated when household member got small job; expedited SNAP not processed within 7 days; immigrant household denied SNAP for eligible citizen children

barrier_reference.text: Citizen children in mixed-status households are often eligible even if parents are not — common misconception

intersections_reference.text: WIC, Medicaid, TANF — often co-administered and co-denied

remedies_reference.text: Reinstatement; back benefits; emergency SNAP through court order

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: SNAP ABAWD (Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents) work requirement rules in active litigation. Several states expanding work requirements beyond federal minimum. Immigration enforcement creating chilling effect on eligible households — document eligibility proactively.

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: 60 days at each appeal level (plus 5 days for mailing)   |   State Range: Federal court appeal: 60 days from AC denial

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Social Security Act Titles II and XVI; 20 CFR Parts 404 and 416; Mascio v. Colvin; Arakas v. Commissioner

elements.text: Claimant has severe medically determinable impairment(s)
Impairment(s) meet or equal a listed impairment, OR claimant cannot perform past work AND cannot perform any work in national economy given age/education/RFC
Disability expected to last 12+ months or result in death
For SSDI: sufficient work credits. For SSI: income/resource limits met.

proof_reference.text: Five-step sequential evaluation. RFC (Residual Functional Capacity) assessment critical. Medical-vocational grid rules. Treating source opinion weight under post-2017 rules. Consultative examination limitations.

fact_patterns.text: Initial denial without examination; ALJ rejecting treating doctor opinion without adequate explanation; hearing decision ignoring documented mental health limitations; grid rules applied incorrectly for age/education

barrier_reference.text: Unrepresented claimants have far worse outcomes at ALJ hearings — legal aid representation is the single biggest factor. SSI: does NOT apply in territories.

intersections_reference.text: Medicaid (SSI categorical eligibility), Medicare (SSDI after 24 months), disability discrimination, Olmstead

remedies_reference.text: Award of benefits; back benefits; attorney fees (25% of back benefits, up to $7,200 — paid from back benefits award)

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: ALJ hearing wait times 12-18+ months. SSA facing staffing reductions. Legal representation at ALJ stage critical. For territory residents: SSDI applies; SSI does not.

claims.canonical_name: ICWA Violation — Improper State Court Child Custody Proceeding
claims.identity_basis: Manually reconciled source identifier and full claim title to the retrieved claim_catalog row; existing ID retained.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Tribal/Indigenous   |   Primary Agency: Tribal court (primary jurisdiction on/near reservation); BIA; state court (must comply with ICWA); ACF

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: Act immediately — ICWA applies at the moment of the proceeding   |   State Range: Immediate action required — intervene in state proceeding

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: N/A

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: ICWA 25 USC §1901; BIA ICWA Guidelines (2015/2016); Haaland v. Brackeen (2023, ICWA constitutional); 25 CFR Part 23

elements.text: Child is an 'Indian child' under ICWA (member of or eligible for membership in federally recognized tribe AND has biological parent who is tribal member)
State child custody proceeding is pending (foster care, termination of parental rights, adoptive placement)
Required ICWA procedures were not followed (notice to tribe, BIA; active efforts; placement preferences; expert witnesses; higher standards of proof)

proof_reference.text: ICWA mandates: (1) notice to tribe and BIA for any Indian child custody proceeding; (2) active efforts (beyond reasonable efforts) to prevent family breakup; (3) placement preferences (extended family → other tribal members → other Indian families); (4) qualified expert witness on tribal child-rearing standards; (5) beyond reasonable doubt standard for TPR.

fact_patterns.text: State agency failed to inquire about tribal membership; tribe not notified of foster care proceeding; placement made with non-Native family without exhausting placement preferences; TPR pursued without active efforts documentation

barrier_reference.text: States (especially SD — documented violations) with history of non-compliance. Tribal enrollment verification delays. Child welfare agencies not asking about tribal membership at intake.

intersections_reference.text: ADA Title II (disability of parent as factor), VAWA (DV-involved families), state child welfare due process

remedies_reference.text: Invalidation of state court orders not complying with ICWA; transfer to tribal court; placement with tribal family members

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) upheld ICWA against equal protection, anticommandeering, and other challenges. ICWA constitutional and binding. South Dakota under federal monitoring for ICWA compliance. BIA ICWA compliance oversight active.

agency_reference.text: Domain: Immigration Intersection   |   Primary Agency: EEOC (employment, 15+); HHS-OCR (healthcare); ED-OCR (schools); HUD (housing); DOJ CRT (pattern; LEP enforcement); state agencies

deadline_reference.text: Federal SOL: EEOC: 300 days; agency complaints: 180 days   |   State Range: Varies

coverage_reference.text: Employer Size: Employment: 15+. Services (Title VI): all federally funded entities

authority_reference.text: Key Statutes: Title VII §703 (national origin); Title VI 42 USC §2000d; Former EO 13166 (revoked by EO 14224 on March 1, 2025); 28 CFR Part 42 (DOJ LEP guidance)

elements.text: Person has limited English proficiency (LEP) or was discriminated against based on national origin/accent
Defendant receives federal funding (or is employer with 15+)
Person was denied meaningful access to services due to language, OR subjected to adverse action because of national origin/accent
Language policy was not justified by business necessity (employment) or had discriminatory intent (services)

proof_reference.text: Executive Order 13166 was revoked by Executive Order 14224 on March 1, 2025. The new order does not itself require agencies to end services in other languages and must be implemented consistently with applicable law. Language-assistance obligations must be checked under the law, regulations and current rules that apply to the particular program; do not rely on the revoked order as current authority. Employment decisions based on accent may violate Title VII. EEOC guidance permits reliance on an accent only where the employer has evidence that effective spoken English is required for the job and the accent materially interferes with that communication; customer or coworker preference is insufficient.

fact_patterns.text: Hospital refusing to provide interpreter — relying on child to interpret; school refusing to translate IEP documents; government agency not providing translated notices; employer terminating employee for accent despite adequate communication; employee harassed for speaking Spanish

barrier_reference.text: Executive Order 13166 was revoked by Executive Order 14224 on March 1, 2025. The new order does not itself require agencies to end services in other languages and must be implemented consistently with applicable law. Language-assistance obligations must be checked under the law, regulations and current rules that apply to the particular program; do not rely on the revoked order as current authority. DOJ states that LEP.gov operations are suspended pending review. Status checked 2026-09-13.

intersections_reference.text: Race/ethnicity discrimination, immigration enforcement chilling effect, EMTALA, IDEA

remedies_reference.text: Employment: Title VII remedies. Services: corrective action, injunctive relief, civil penalties (federal funding termination as ultimate remedy)

dated_note.text: 2025 NOTE: Immigration enforcement climate creating chilling effect on LEP communities accessing services — health, education, housing. Document access barriers even if person declines to file.

barriers.name: Mandatory Arbitration Agreement

description.text: Pre-dispute arbitration agreements in employment contracts or as condition of employment that waive right to court. May also prohibit class actions.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Eliminates federal/state court access; may require individual arbitration instead of EEOC-preserved right to sue. Some arbitration clauses also waive class/collective action rights.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: Check if EEOC charge right is preserved (it is — EEOC can sue on worker's behalf). Check if state law limits enforceability (CA PAGA cannot be waived; IL recent changes). Sexual harassment/assault arbitration waivers banned by Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act (2022).

applicability_questions: Does a relevant agreement exist, and what claims and parties does it cover?
Which forum, statutory exceptions and enforceability rules govern this agreement?

barriers.name: At-Will Employment Doctrine

description.text: Default US rule: employer can terminate for any reason or no reason, as long as not an illegal reason.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Creates 'pretext' burden — must show termination was for illegal reason, not just arbitrary reason.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: Circumstantial evidence: temporal proximity; comparator evidence; employer shifting explanations; pretext argument. Focus on timeline and documentation of protected activity.

applicability_questions: Was there termination or another adverse employment action?
What jurisdiction, contract and claimed protected activity apply?

barriers.name: Qualified Immunity

description.text: Doctrine shielding government officials from §1983 liability unless they violated 'clearly established' constitutional right.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Effectively immunizes most individual officer defendants even for serious constitutional violations. Case against agency (municipality — Monell) is usually more viable.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: Monell claim against municipality (policy or custom causing violation). State tort claims often not subject to qualified immunity. State law civil rights claims in states that have abolished or limited qualified immunity (CO, NM, NJ, NY, MA).

applicability_questions: Is the defendant an individual official, municipality, state or another entity?
What claim and form of relief are asserted? Immunities cannot be transferred between them.

barriers.name: Administrative Exhaustion Requirement

description.text: Must complete administrative process (EEOC charge, state agency, Medicaid fair hearing) before filing in court.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Missing administrative deadline forecloses court access. Procedural trap for unrepresented claimants.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: File administrative charge immediately at intake — SOL protection even if investigation capacity limited. Do not wait to gather all evidence before filing charge.

applicability_questions: Which administrative process is required for this specific cause of action and remedy?
What notice, event date, prior filing and exception evidence exists?

barriers.name: ERISA Preemption (Employee Benefits)

description.text: ERISA preempts most state law claims relating to employer-provided benefit plans (health, disability, pension).

impact_reference.text: Impact: State tort claims, state contract claims, and punitive damages generally unavailable for self-funded employer plan claims. Limited to ERISA equitable remedies.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: ERISA parity claims (MHPAEA); ERISA §502(a) breach of fiduciary duty; §510 retaliation. State insurance laws apply to fully-insured plans (not self-funded). Check whether plan is self-funded or insured.

applicability_questions: What kind of plan is involved, and is it self-funded, insured or outside ERISA?
What benefit, parity or other cause of action and remedy is being considered?

barriers.name: Short Statute of Limitations (Employment)

description.text: Employment discrimination SOLs range from 120 days (DE) to 6 years (MN). Most are 180-300 days administrative.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Claims are permanently barred after SOL. Missing by one day = no claim. Equitable tolling limited.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: File EEOC charge on DAY ONE of intake. Do not wait. State agencies with longer SOLs may preserve claims federal SOL has cut off.

applicability_questions: Which forum and event starts each potentially relevant clock?
Are there independent clocks, receipt dates, tolling or preserved filings requiring review?

barriers.name: No State Remedy (Civil Rights Gap States)

description.text: AL, MS, GA (private), NC (private), AR have no effective state employment civil rights enforcement for private sector.

impact_reference.text: Impact: EEOC exclusively. No state agency investigation. For employers under 15: virtually no remedy.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: 42 USC §1981 for race claims (no size minimum, 4yr SOL, no damage caps). FLSA/NLRA for wage and concerted activity. State tort: WDPOP, IIED. Private bar referral.

applicability_questions: What jurisdiction, employer type, size and protected basis apply?
Does a court remedy exist even if an administrative enforcement office does not?

barriers.name: Immigration Status Fear

description.text: Undocumented or mixed-status workers and families may fear filing complaints due to immigration enforcement concerns.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Systematic underreporting of labor, housing, and civil rights violations in immigrant communities.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: FLSA, NLRA, EEOC explicitly protect workers regardless of immigration status. Confidentiality protocols. Provide information in native language. Community organizations as bridges. U-visa for crime victims who cooperate with law enforcement.

applicability_questions: What safe language and communication access does the person want?
What program-specific eligibility, confidentiality and reporting rules require review? Do not infer immigration status.

barriers.name: Proof of Intent (Employment Discrimination)

description.text: Most employment discrimination claims require proving discriminatory intent, not just bad outcome.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Circumstantial evidence required in most cases. Direct evidence rare. McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting is the primary framework.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: Document: comparator employees; supervisor comments; shifts in treatment after protected activity; employer's inconsistent explanations; statistical evidence of workforce demographics.

applicability_questions: Which theory requires intent, causation or a different standard?
What comparator, timing, direct statement or record evidence exists?

barriers.name: Federal Enforcement Reduction (2025)

description.text: EEOC, DOJ CRT, CFPB, ED-OCR all operating at significantly reduced enforcement capacity under 2025 administration changes.

impact_reference.text: Impact: Charges may not be investigated; right to sue letters issued quickly without investigation; consent decrees ended.

mitigation_reference.text: Mitigation: File federal charges to preserve rights + pursue state agencies aggressively + consider private litigation faster than prior years.

applicability_questions: What current operational evidence establishes agency capacity or intake availability?
Which independent filing or community-support options remain available? Source 2025 observations are not current verification.

review_issues.reason: ECOA limitations assertion requires current primary-authority review. Do not convert to a deadline.
Blanket SSI territory exclusion conflicts with supplied American Samoa directory treatment of CNMI; resolve program and jurisdiction individually.
Title III entry combines a web accessibility rule with a note expressly distinguishing Title II and Title III. Do not transfer a Title II rule to Title III.
No state remedy/EEOC exclusively language must distinguish administrative agency availability, court remedy, employer coverage and alternative causes.
Exhaustion and missed-deadline outcomes are overbroad without claim/forum/trigger/exception review. No universal day-one filing instruction or expired-case verdict.
Federal capacity assertions are explicitly dated 2025; current agency operation and available alternatives remain unverified.
Causation, remedy, numerical duration, eligibility and status assertions need pinpoint primary-authority review before use as legal conclusions.
Language-access passages have an explicit later status-check date. Preserve this sample version separately from unmatched enriched source variants.

Qualified immunity is a separate Section 1983 topic. No exact Section 1983 claim exists in these 27 detailed entries; do not treat an ADA Title II claim as equivalent. Connect the existing Section 1983 catalog only after its elements and defendant/remedy scope are reviewed.
